content.title: About
content.content: Coffee creamer is a liquid additive designed to enhance the flavor and texture of coffee. This fat‑free version contains no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets. It is typically based on water, milk proteins, flavorings, and sweeteners.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Liquid creamers are widely used in cafés and restaurants for quick beverage preparation.
The fat‑free version reduces the calorie count of a cup of coffee by about 30–40 % compared with traditional cream.
Some brands fortify the product with vitamin D and calcium for added nutritional value.
Creamers can be flavored with vanilla, caramel, nutty notes, and other tastes.
It mixes easily even in cold drinks such as iced lattes.

items.title: Calorie reduction
items.content: The absence of fat lowers the overall calorie content, which is helpful for weight management.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Added calcium and vitamin D contribute to stronger bones.

items.title: Sweet taste without sugar
items.content: Sweeteners provide sweetness without raising blood glucose levels.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Lack of fat makes the product gentler on the stomach, especially for those with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some creamers contain whey protein, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Excessive intake can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain variants may have higher salt levels, which should be considered by people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 10–30 ml of creamer to hot or cold coffee to taste. It can be used for lattes, cappuccinos, frappés, and dessert drinks. Multiple flavor variants can be combined if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 7–10 days. Do not freeze. Discard if color, smell, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: This cookie combines dark chocolate, rolled oats and shredded coconut, requires no baking and is ready in minutes. The texture is soft with a slight crunch, and the flavor is rich chocolate with hints of coconut and oat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats give the cookie extra fiber and help it hold together without baking.
Coconut adds a fragrant tropical note and healthy fats.
The chocolate can be dark or milk, depending on preference.
The cookie sets in the refrigerator, making it an ideal summer treat.
No‑bake preparation preserves more nutrients, especially from the oats.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Oats contain soluble fiber that supports digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Coconut provides medium‑chain triglycerides that are quickly metabolized for energy.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate is high in flavonoids, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: The mix of monounsaturated fats from coconut and fiber from oats can support healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Mood boost
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can improve mood and increase energy.

items.title: Nut and coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to coconut or ingredients in the chocolate.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cookie is calorie‑dense due to fats and sugar, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: If sweetened chocolate is used, the sugar level can be high, which may be unsuitable for diabetics.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: Rolled oats may contain trace gluten unless certified gluten‑free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cookie is convenient as a standalone snack, added to yogurt, ice cream, or used as a base for dessert plates. Keep it chilled to maintain its firmness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag and thaw at room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna is a marine predatory fish of the Scombridae family, found in warm and temperate ocean waters. Raw tuna has a firm, slightly pink flesh with a mild flavor and moderate fat content. It is commonly used in sushi, sashimi, steaks, and also canned after cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna can migrate thousands of kilometers, moving between tropical and temperate zones.
The largest species, the bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus), can exceed 600 kg in weight.
Tuna is rich in protein and omega‑3 fatty acids, making it popular among athletes.
In Japan, tuna is a prized delicacy with centuries‑old fishing traditions.
Tuna can maintain a body temperature higher than the surrounding water thanks to a specialized circulatory system.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Raw tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support heart health, vascular function, and brain development.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Tuna supplies all essential amino acids, beneficial for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, tuna contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is a good source of B12, B6, and niacin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish provides selenium, magnesium, and phosphorus, important for antioxidant protection and bone health.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Large tuna species can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tuna.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw fish can harbor pathogenic bacteria; using fresh product and proper hygiene is essential.

items.title: Storage issues
items.content: Improper storage leads to rapid quality loss, off‑odors, and off‑flavors.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw tuna is ideal for sashimi, rolls, poke bowls, and salads. It is sliced thinly and often served with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger. It can also be lightly marinated in citrus or vinegar before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tuna in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, tightly wrapped in a sealed container or film. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C using vacuum‑sealed packaging. Thaw frozen tuna in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Queso Cotija is a hard, dry Mexican cheese made from cow's milk. It has a sharp, salty flavor and a crumbly texture similar to Parmesan. It is commonly used as a topping to add a burst of flavor to dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese is named after the town of Cotija in the state of Michoacán, where it was traditionally produced.
Cotija is often compared to Parmesan, but its taste is more pungent and salty.
The cheese is aged from several weeks to several months, depending on the desired intensity.
In Mexico, Cotija is used in classic dishes such as elote, tacos, salsas, and Mexican salads.
It is usually sold in small blocks that are crumbled right before serving.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cotija provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: It contains over 600 mg of calcium per 100 g, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The cheese supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low lactose
items.content: During long aging the lactose level drops, making Cotija often tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: It includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cotija is very salty; individuals with hypertension should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: As a dairy product, it can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Its fat content makes it calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cotija is typically crumbled or grated and sprinkled over tacos, soups, salads, beans, grilled corn (elote), and vegetable dishes. It can also be added to sauces or baked dishes to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Cotija in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2 °C–4 °C. For longer storage it can be frozen, though the texture becomes more crumbly. Discard the cheese if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Teriyaki sauce is a sweet‑savory Japanese condiment made from soy sauce, sake (or mirin), sugar, and ginger. It is used as a marinade, glaze, and seasoning for meat, fish, vegetables, and rice dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teriyaki means “bright sauce,” referring to its glossy, shiny finish after cooking.
The traditional recipe includes rice wine (sake) and mirin, but many commercial versions use corn syrup.
In Japan the sauce is often made at home, while in the US and Europe it became popular as a ready‑to‑use product.
Teriyaki can be light or dark; the dark version contains more soy sauce and caramelized sugar.
Vegetarian versions exist that omit fish ingredients and rely solely on plant‑based components.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy sauce, the base of teriyaki, provides plant‑based protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Ginger and garlic, common additions, are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger stimulates gastric secretions, aiding digestion.

items.title: Lower sodium options available
items.content: Some modern recipes use low‑sodium soy sauce, reducing overall salt intake.

items.title: Adds flavor without excess fat
items.content: Teriyaki imparts a strong taste, allowing reduced oil use when cooking.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Teriyaki sauce often contains a significant amount of sugar, which can increase calories and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Traditional soy sauce is high in sodium; people with hypertension should choose reduced‑salt versions.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid teriyaki sauce or use alternatives based on coconut aminos.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some commercial sauces add MSG, which may cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Teriyaki sauce works well for marinating chicken, beef, pork, and tofu, as a glaze for grilling, in stir‑fries, as a dipping sauce for sushi rolls, and as a dip for vegetables. It can be thinned with water or broth for a lighter consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store teriyaki sauce in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator after opening. It typically remains good for 6–12 months. Discard if the smell, color, or texture changes or if sediment appears.
